section_summary: This section (pages 1-70) contains diplomatic despatches, press translations, and State Department memoranda concerning the political crisis in Japan following the February 26, 1936 military coup d'état. It documents Chinese and international reactions to the assassinations of key statesmen, intelligence on the trial of Lieutenant Colonel Saburo Aizawa and the conspirators behind the rebellion, and Dr. H. H. Kung's confidential warnings regarding Japanese global imperial ambitions. The documents trace the contentious negotiations surrounding the formation of Koki Hirota's Cabinet, which was heavily constrained by military vetoes, and analyze the Cabinet's subsequent policy platform capitulating to the Army's demands for national defense expansion, state-controlled economic reforms, and an aggressive foreign policy.

subfiles.about: Continuation of an American Embassy Peiping despatch transmitting translations of Chinese press editorials regarding the February 26 coup d'état in Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: Contains embassy translations of Chinese press editorials analyzing the February 26 Incident in Tokyo. An editorial from the Pei Jih Pao examines the military mutiny, the assassinations of leading statesmen, the internal political motives of the young officers, and the repercussions for Britain, the USSR, and China. A second editorial extract reviews the international implications of the violent revolt, expressing skepticism that Japanese foreign policy will fundamentally alter given existing military dominance.
subfiles.title: Chinese Press Comments on the Tokyo Coup d'État of February 26, 1936

subfiles.about: Despatch forwarding an editorial translation from the Nanking newspaper Hsin Min Pao analyzing the future of Japan after the February 26 Incident.
subfiles.from: Willys R. Peck, Counselor of Embassy, Nanking
subfiles.summary: Counselor of Embassy Willys R. Peck transmits an editorial entitled 'The Future of Japan' published in the Nanking Hsin Min Pao on March 3, 1936. Peck notes that Chinese press comment has been restrained, possibly due to censorship, and highlights the writer's observation that the revolt reflects the decay of a law-governed state and the wilful action of a military faction rather than a broad political movement. The editorial itself critiques the rebellious military officers, details their forced surrender by Imperial order, and warns of the dangers of military fascism while expressing hope that Japanese civilian society and political parties might check military extremism.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 123: Chinese Comment on the Tokyo Incident of February 26, 1936

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum summarizing Shanghai newspaper comment and remarks by T. V. Soong on the formation and prospects of the new Hirota Cabinet.
subfiles.from: John Carter Vincent, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: John Carter Vincent summarizes Shanghai Consulate General Despatch No. 77, reviewing reactions in the English-language and Chinese vernacular press to the new Japanese Cabinet under Koki Hirota. The memorandum highlights press predictions that the Army will dominate the Cabinet, notes dissatisfaction with the appointment of Eiichi Baba as Finance Minister, and reports remarks by T. V. Soong warning that recent developments will accelerate Japanese aggression and that hostilities may break out soon.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Shanghai Despatch No. 77: Newspaper Comment on the New Japanese Cabinet
subfiles.to: Erle R. Dickover, Division of Far Eastern Affairs

subfiles.about: Despatch transmitting a copy of Shanghai Despatch No. 70 to Peiping and local press editorials on the February 26 Incident and the Hirota Cabinet.
subfiles.from: Clarence E. Gauss, American Consul General, Shanghai
subfiles.summary: Consul General Clarence E. Gauss transmits a copy of his Despatch No. 70 to the American Embassy at Peiping, reporting Shanghai press opinion regarding the February 26 Incident and the formation of the Hirota Cabinet. Enclosed editorials from the Shanghai Evening Post and Mercury, The Shanghai Times, and other sources analyze the Army's dominance in cabinet-making, compromises forced upon Premier Koki Hirota, the financial implications of Eiichi Baba's appointment, and the threat of increased Japanese military aggression in China.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 77: Sino-Japanese Relations: Shanghai Opinion on February 26 Incident. Selection of New Cabinet

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum analyzing Tokyo Embassy Despatch No. 1735 on the extent to which the February 26 insurgents achieved their aims.
subfiles.from: Erle R. Dickover, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: Erle R. Dickover comments on Despatch No. 1735 prepared by George D. Andrews of the Tokyo Embassy regarding the degree of success attained by the February 26 rebels. The memorandum notes that while the despatch concludes the insurgents' successful aims outweighed their failures, it does not distinguish between foreign and domestic policy objectives, leaving unanswered the key question of whether chauvinism in Japan is on the rise or decline.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 1735: Measure of Success Achieved by the February 26 Insurgents
subfiles.to: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Chief, Division of Far Eastern Affairs

subfiles.about: Despatch analyzing how the February 26 insurrection stimulated the Japanese Government to adopt many reforms demanded by the military rebels.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew transmits an analysis prepared by George D. Andrews evaluating the success and failure of the February 26 insurgents' aims. The report details how, despite the military suppression and punishment of rebel officers, the new Hirota Government and War Minister Terauchi embraced core rebel demands, including clarifying national polity, expanding military budgets, rejecting Meiji liberalism, and promoting state-controlled economic reforms. The despatch concludes that the successful aims outweighed those that failed, ultimately accelerating the breakdown of Japan's political status quo.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1735: An Analysis of the Measure of Success Achieved by the February 26 Insurgents

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum summarizing Tokyo Despatch No. 1746 regarding the court-martial of Lieutenant Colonel Aizawa and upcoming trials of February 26 rebels.
subfiles.from: William T. Turner, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: William T. Turner summarizes a report from the Tokyo Embassy concerning the suspension and required retrial of Lieutenant Colonel Saburo Aizawa for the murder of Major General Tetsuzan Nagata. The memorandum highlights reports that forthcoming trials of February 26 participants will be conducted strictly in camera without public airing of political ideologies to expedite establishing legal guilt.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 1746: Trial of Lieutenant Colonel Aizawa
subfiles.to: Erle R. Dickover and Maxwell M. Hamilton, Division of Far Eastern Affairs

subfiles.about: Despatch reporting on the trial of Lieutenant Colonel Aizawa, the key civilian and military conspirators behind the February 26 revolt, and military judicial procedures.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew reports developments connecting the court-martial of Lieutenant Colonel Saburo Aizawa with the February 26 Incident, noting information from the War Office identifying Koji Muranaka, Asaichi Isobe, Zei Nishida, and Kazuteru Kita as the true ringleaders behind the rebellion. The despatch describes Kita's influential nationalist writings, notes the procedural suspension requiring Aizawa's retrial, and explains that subsequent trials of February 26 participants will be held secretly in camera without defense counsel or rights of appeal. It also reports an upcoming conference of Army and Division commanders scheduled for April 7 to unify military discipline.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1746: Trial of Lieutenant Colonel Aizawa and Its Connection with the February 26 Incident

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum summarizing remarks by Dr. H. H. Kung concerning Japanese imperial ambitions, naval expansion, and collective security.
subfiles.from: John Carter Vincent, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: John Carter Vincent outlines remarks made by Chinese Finance Minister H. H. Kung to Ambassador Nelson T. Johnson. Kung warned that Japanese militarists envision a global empire rivaling Great Britain's, noted strategic divisions between the Japanese Army's continental expansion and the Navy's South Pacific ambitions, and emphasized the necessity of collective international action to curb Japanese aggression.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Nanking Despatch No. 112: Conversation with Dr. H. H. Kung on Japanese Imperialism
subfiles.to: Maxwell M. Hamilton and Robin O. Miller, Division of Far Eastern Affairs

subfiles.about: Despatch transmitting a memorandum of conversation with Chinese Finance Minister Dr. H. H. Kung regarding Japanese world ambitions and regional designs.
subfiles.from: Willys R. Peck, Counselor of Embassy, Nanking (for Nelson T. Johnson)
subfiles.summary: Counselor of Embassy Willys R. Peck transmits a memorandum of a March 5, 1936 conversation between Dr. H. H. Kung, Vice President of the Executive Yuan and Minister of Finance, and Ambassador Nelson T. Johnson. Dr. Kung expressed concern over Western complacency toward Japanese expansionism, asserting that Japanese militarists seek worldwide empire through controlling China. Kung outlined conflicting expansion strategies between the Japanese Army (continental expansion against China and the USSR) and Navy (expansion toward the South Pacific), while also discussing Japanese economic penetration and the need for international collective security.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 112: Japanese Imperialistic Ambitions

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum summarizing Tokyo Despatch No. 1736 regarding the political maneuvering leading to the formation of the Hirota Cabinet.
subfiles.from: William T. Turner, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: William T. Turner notes receipt of Tokyo Despatch No. 1736 detailing the chronological steps and behind-the-scenes negotiations involved in establishing the Hirota Cabinet. Turner observes that the despatch was drafted prior to Hachiro Arita assuming the Foreign Ministry and provides useful background on political developments.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 1736: Formation of the Hirota Cabinet
subfiles.to: Erle R. Dickover, Division of Far Eastern Affairs

subfiles.about: Internal State Department file routing and cross-reference sheet for records indexed under decimal file 894.00/636.
subfiles.summary: A Department of State Division of Far Eastern Affairs record cross-reference slip indicating file indexing and tallying records for decimal file 894.00/636 and related classifications.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet: Decimal File 894.00/636

subfiles.about: Despatch providing a detailed chronological account of the political crisis, military intervention, and negotiations resulting in the formation of the Hirota Cabinet.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew transmits a report prepared by Cabot Coville tracing the formation of the new Japanese Cabinet following the February 26 Incident. The despatch chronicles Prince Fumimaro Konoye's refusal of the premiership, Koki Hirota's designation, and intense opposition from the military—led by prospective War Minister General Juichi Terauchi—against proposed ministers such as Shigeru Yoshida, Hiroshi Shimomura, and Naoshi Ohara. It details how compromise was reached through the mediation of Eiichi Baba, leading to the formal installation of the Hirota Cabinet on March 9, 1936, with significant military influence over ministerial appointments.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1736: Formation of the Hirota Cabinet

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum summarizing Tokyo Despatch No. 1733 on the policy platform of the Hirota Cabinet and Japanese public reaction.
subfiles.from: William T. Turner, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: William T. Turner summarizes Tokyo Despatch No. 1733 prepared by Erle R. Dickover concerning the official statement of policy issued by the Hirota Cabinet on March 17, 1936. The memorandum explains that the platform incorporates the Army's four key conditions: eradicating liberalism/internationalism, expanding national defense, enacting state-controlled economic and social reforms, and pursuing a positive foreign policy toward China and the USSR. It also highlights Hirota's assurances of friendly relations with the United States and the unenthusiastic reaction of the Japanese public.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 1733: Policy of the Hirota Cabinet and Public Opinion
subfiles.to: Stanley K. Hornbeck and Under Secretary of State

subfiles.about: Despatch analyzing the policy statement of the Hirota Cabinet and its alignment with the Army's four fundamental demands.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew transmits a detailed study prepared by Erle R. Dickover examining the March 17, 1936 statement of policy issued by the new Hirota Cabinet. The despatch analyzes how the platform capitulated to the Army's core demands: clarifying the national polity against the Minobe 'Emperor-organ' theory, expanding military armaments against the Soviet Union, stabilising livelihood through state control and tax reform, and enacting an independent, positive foreign policy in East Asia. Grew explains that civil authorities accepted these terms as an essential compromise to maintain governance and avoid a more radical military dictatorship.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1733: The Policy of the Hirota Cabinet and Public Opinion Thereanent
